extracted.intended_audience: EPA decisionmakers, administrative law attorneys, environmental public-interest organizations, and parties challenging EPA rulemakings
extracted.subtask_description: A statutory petition asking EPA to convene mandatory reconsideration under Clean Air Act §307(d)(7)(B) of aspects of a final rule that were not adequately noticed in the proposal and that are centrally relevant to the rule’s outcome. The document explains the legal standard, identifies allegedly new and flawed technical analyses introduced in the final rule, and requests reopening for public comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory standard for mandatory reconsideration (CAA §307(d)(7)(B))
rubrics_metrics.description: Only an objection to a rule or procedure which was raised with reasonable specificity during the period for public comment (including any public hearing) may be raised during judicial review. If the person raising an objection can demonstrate to the Administrator that it was impracticable to raise such objection within such time or if the grounds for such objection arose after the period for public comment (but within the time specified for judicial review) and if such objection is of central relevance to the outcome of the rule, the Administrator shall convene a proceeding for reconsideration of the rule and provide the same procedural rights as would have been afforded had the information been available at the time the rule was proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute’s mandatory 'shall' requires EPA to convene reconsideration upon a required demonstration. Reconsideration grants the public an opportunity to timely comment on important aspects of a final rule that were not properly noticed in a proposed rule. An objection is covered if it was impracticable to raise during the comment period or arose after the comment period but is of central relevance to the rule’s outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as 'impracticable to raise' / timing ground
rubrics_metrics.description: An objection is 'impracticable to raise' if it could not reasonably have been raised during the public comment period (including where the grounds for objection arose after the period for public comment but within the time for judicial review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a final rule introduces analyses, methodologies, data, or legal rationales that were not disclosed in the proposal, affected parties cannot practicably have raised objections during the comment period; such objections therefore qualify for mandatory reconsideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central relevance test
rubrics_metrics.description: An objection is of 'central relevance' if it 'provides substantial support for the argument that the regulation should be revised' and objections that 'go to the very legality' of the Final Rule satisfy this test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an objection challenges the legality or core factual basis of the rule and could materially affect the outcome, it is centrally relevant and warrants reconsideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice requirements for proposed rule (CAA §307(d)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed rule notice 'shall be accompanied by a statement of its basis and purpose,' including 'the factual data on which the proposed rule is based; ... the methodology used in obtaining the data and in analyzing the data; and ... the major ... policy considerations underlying the proposed rule.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These notice requirements are designed to ensure agency regulations are tested by public comment, to ensure fairness to affected parties, and to allow parties to develop evidence in the record. If the final rule deviates too sharply from the proposal (i.e., not a logical outgrowth), meaningful notice has not been provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical outgrowth / deviation-from-proposal standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A final rule that deviates too sharply from the proposal does not provide meaningful notice under §307(d)(3); ambiguous comments or weak signals from the agency do not suffice to put parties on notice of a significant change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alterations in a final rule must be something parties should have anticipated based on the proposal itself. The agency may not 'bootstrap' notice from other commenters' analyses; EPA itself must provide notice of material changes. Where analyses supporting a final conclusion were not disclosed in the proposal, mandatory reconsideration is proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of factual data, methodology, and quantitative assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency relies on technical analyses, models, data, or quantitative assumptions to support rule conclusions, those materials (the factual data, the methodology used, and major policy considerations) must be presented in the proposal so commenters can respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introducing new models, data, or key assumptions only in the final rule deprives the public of the ability to scrutinize and comment; such late introduction is a ground for reconsideration. Examples cited include EPA’s new modeling of emissions, GMST, and GSLR, and an 'illustrative' 50% scenario that were not in the proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on relying on commenters' analyses to supply agency notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency cannot rely on analyses submitted by commenters to establish that the agency provided adequate notice of a new approach or analysis; EPA itself must provide notice of its regulatory proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having failed to provide notice itself, the agency cannot 'bootstrap' notice from public comments or claimant-submitted materials. The public comment period is intended to respond to the agency’s proposal and supporting materials, not to the content of other public comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate treatment of modeling and technical analysis in rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Modeling and technical analyses that are foundational to the agency’s factual determinations must be disclosed, justified, and open to public comment; modeling choices (parameters, scenarios, metrics) must be explained and defensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling that was created after the comment period or that uses analytic tools 'not intended for this purpose' (e.g., EPA’s admitted use of back-of-the-envelope 50% illustrative reductions) cannot be the basis for final conclusions without giving notice and an opportunity to comment. Modeling parameters are highly sensitive and agency choices must be supported; failure to expose assumptions is a serious deficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: De minimis yardsticks used by EPA (as described in Final Rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA compares U.S. vehicle impacts against three alleged de minimis yardsticks: (i) the 'range of measurability' of global temperature and sea level rise; (ii) global temperature 'variability' for 2016–2025; and (iii) a 1% contribution threshold (EPA asserts courts have consistently viewed 1% as de minimis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The petition argues these yardsticks were introduced in the Final Rule (not the proposal), are conceptually inappropriate, numerically erroneous, and in the case of the 1% threshold, lack judicial support; whether impacts exceed these yardsticks is a core factual determination central to the rule’s legality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to measuring contribution and futility
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s futility rationale measures the percentage contribution of U.S. vehicle CO2 emissions to global mean surface temperature (GMST) and global sea level rise (GSLR) and then tests whether those percentages are 'measurable' or 'material' compared to the de minimis yardsticks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The petitioners assert that (a) the statute requires finding 'contribution' to dangerous air pollution, not a prerequisite showing that regulation would materially affect the danger; (b) reliance solely on global-average metrics can obscure domestic harms; and (c) EPA’s new focus on CO2 and these particular global metrics was not included in the proposal and so required reconsideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for agency reversal of longstanding analytic/policy practice
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency reverses a longstanding policy or practice (e.g., monetizing ozone and PM2.5 co-benefits), it must acknowledge the change and provide a more detailed and reasoned justification than would be required on a blank slate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations (e.g., FCC v. Fox) require the agency to explain the specific factual premises and reasoning underlying the prior policy and why departure is justified. A brief, unexplained abandonment of long-standing monetization practices (or wholesale treating of benefits as zero) fails the reasoned-explanation requirement and is arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to quantify benefits to the fullest extent practicable (EO 12866 / EPA Guidelines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive Order 12,866 and EPA’s own Guidelines for Preparing Economic Analyses require EPA to quantify health and other benefits to the fullest extent possible and to use established guidance unless adequately explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must justify departures from its Guidelines and cannot 'zero out' health co-benefits absent strong scientific justification. Established methods and Science Advisory Board vetting are relevant and must be acknowledged when changing course. Refusing to monetize benefits without adequate explanation skews cost–benefit comparisons and is arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative discre­tion to reconsider under APA §553(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if mandatory reconsideration under CAA §307(d)(7)(B) is not met, the agency has discretion to reconsider its actions under Administrative Procedure Act §553(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners request reconsideration both as mandatory under §307(d)(7)(B) and, alternatively, under APA §553(e) to correct errors and ensure public input when new analyses are presented only in a final rule.
